why_how.text: Suspension and revocation both take away your driving privilege, but they end in very different ways.
Some offenses force a suspension or revocation, and others only permit one.

scenario.text: Lou's privilege was revoked, and the revocation term has ended.

reasoning.text: Revocation ends the privilege outright: restoration means re-applying after the term with legal presence proof, fresh vision, two-part knowledge and road tests, plus fees.

result.text: Lou re-applies, proves legal presence, retakes the vision, knowledge and road tests, and pays the fees.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a revocation ends and the license simply comes back, as with a suspension.

correction.text: Suspension parks the privilege for fees and presence proofs, while revocation ends it outright and demands re-applying with full retests.

prompt.text: Lou's revocation term is over. What must Lou do to drive again?

answer.text: Re-apply with legal presence proof, vision, knowledge and road tests, plus fees.

rationale.text: Revocation ends the privilege outright, so restoration means re-applying with full retests, unlike a suspension.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on penalties. Your driving privilege can be suspended or revoked, and the manual explains the difference and how each one is restored. It then lists the offenses for which courts or DMV must suspend or revoke a license, and the offenses for which a court may do so. By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain what each word means, what you must do to drive again after each one, and which offenses fall on the must list and which on the may list. Listen for the words must and may, because they separate the two lists.

lines.text: Parks the privilege for a time.
Pay up and prove legal presence to reclaim it.
Expired over a year: repass the exams.

narration.text: A suspension takes away your privilege for a period of time. Afterward, you reclaim it by paying the required fees and proving legal presence. There is one extra condition: if your license expired more than a year ago while it was suspended, you must also repass the two-part knowledge exam, the road test and the vision test. So suspension parks the privilege for a while, and getting it back usually means fees and presence proof. Keep the expired-license condition in mind, because it is the one case in which a suspension also brings back the full set of exams that a revocation always requires, as the next slide shows.

lines.text: Legal presence, vision, knowledge, road tests, fees.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver whose privilege was revoked may think it simply comes back when the term ends, as a suspension does. It does not. Revocation ends the privilege outright. Restoration means re-applying after the term, with legal presence proof, a fresh vision test, the two-part knowledge test and the road test, plus fees. So suspension parks the privilege for fees and presence proofs, while revocation ends it and demands re-applying with full retests. The memory line is: suspended parks, revoked restarts. A revoked driver goes back through the vision, knowledge and road tests, rather than simply paying and returning to the road.

lines.text: DUI, DUI injury, driving on DUI suspension.
Skipping a required interlock; lying to DMV.
Hit-and-run with injury; manslaughter; felonies; eluding police.

narration.text: Courts or DMV must suspend or revoke for a long list of offenses. The list includes DUI, DUI causing injury, driving while suspended for DUI, skipping a required ignition interlock, lying to DMV, hit-and-run with injury, vehicular manslaughter, DUI manslaughter, drug crimes involving a vehicle, felonies involving a vehicle, impersonating someone at an exam, and eluding police. These are the must-act offenses. Courts may suspend or revoke for reckless or aggressive driving convictions. So DUI, manslaughter, felonies and impersonation force action, while reckless and aggressive driving merely permit it. The word must is what separates the first list from the second.

lines.text: Driving through a non-DUI suspension or revocation.
Refusing blood or breath tests when DUI-charged.

narration.text: The may-suspend list goes on beyond reckless and aggressive driving. It also includes driving without a license, driving through a suspension or revocation that is not for DUI, and refusing blood or breath tests when charged with DUI. So unlicensed driving and test refusal join the may list, while everyday traffic offenses feed the demerit point system, which is the subject of the next lesson. Notice the difference between driving on a DUI suspension, which is on the must list, and driving through a suspension that is not for DUI, which is on the may list. The reason for the original suspension decides which list applies.

Here is a quick check: Lou's driving privilege was revoked, and the revocation term has now ended. What must Lou do to drive again? Work it out before reading on. The answer: re-apply after the term, with legal presence proof, a fresh vision test, the two-part knowledge test and the road test, plus fees. Revocation ends the privilege outright, so it does not simply come back. If Lou's privilege had been suspended instead, Lou would pay up and prove legal presence, and would retest only if the license had expired more than a year during the suspension. Suspended parks; revoked restarts.

To close the lesson: a suspension parks your privilege, and you reclaim it by paying up and proving legal presence, with the exams repeated if your license expired more than a year during the suspension. A revocation ends the privilege outright, and restoration means re-applying after the term with legal presence proof, vision, knowledge and road tests, plus fees. Courts or DMV must suspend or revoke for DUI, manslaughter, vehicle felonies, exam impersonation, eluding police and the other listed offenses. Courts may suspend or revoke for reckless or aggressive driving, unlicensed operation, driving through a non-DUI suspension, and refusing blood or breath tests when charged with DUI.

why_how.text: DMV records every conviction and assigns demerit points, watched over twelve-month and twenty-four-month windows.
Clinics, suspensions and revocations follow set lines that depend on your age and your points.

scenario.text: Zack is twenty-five and builds up eighteen points in twelve months.

reasoning.text: Past eighteen, eighteen points in twelve months suspends ninety days plus the clinic.

result.text: Zack's license is suspended for ninety days, and he must complete the clinic.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking twelve and eighteen points always lead to the same result.

correction.text: Twelve in twelve or eighteen in twenty-four orders the clinic, while eighteen in twelve or twenty-four in twenty-four suspends ninety days.

memory_support.text: Twelve in twelve, clinic; eighteen in twelve, suspension.

prompt.text: Zack, twenty-five, has eighteen points in twelve months. What follows?

answer.text: A ninety-day suspension plus the clinic.

rationale.text: Eighteen points in twelve months or twenty-four in twenty-four suspends ninety days, while twelve in twelve orders the clinic.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on demerit points, clinics and medical review. DMV logs every court conviction for Virginia drivers and assigns demerit points for traffic offenses. Depending on your age and how many points you build up, you may be ordered to a clinic, suspended, or, for younger drivers, revoked. The manual sets different lines for drivers under eighteen, for drivers aged eighteen or nineteen, and for drivers past eighteen by point totals. It also describes medical review, which follows a separate path when there are doubts about a driver's physical or mental fitness. By the end of this lesson you should know the point lines for each group.

lines.text: Three, four or six demerits per traffic offense.

narration.text: DMV logs every court conviction for Virginians, assigns three, four or six demerit points for traffic offenses, and watches twelve-month and twenty-four-month point windows. So points accumulate from convictions, each traffic offense carries three, four or six of them, and the totals are measured over twelve months and over twenty-four months. Compare the may-suspend list from the last lesson: unlicensed driving and test refusal join the may list, while everyday offenses feed the three, four and six point system. The point windows matter because the same total can mean different things depending on whether it built up over twelve months or over twenty-four.

lines.text: First demerit or belt conviction: clinic.
Clinic missed in ninety days: suspended until done, plus a fee.
Second: ninety-day suspension. Third: revoked a year or until eighteen.

narration.text: For drivers under eighteen, the first demerit or seat belt conviction orders a clinic. If the clinic is not completed within ninety days, the license is suspended until it is done, plus a fee. A second conviction suspends the license for ninety days. A third revokes it for a year, or until age eighteen, whichever lasts longer. At eighteen or nineteen, any demerit or belt conviction from those years orders a clinic. So under eighteen stacks a clinic, a ninety-day suspension, then a year revocation across three strikes, while eighteen and nineteen draw only the clinic. Note that seat belt convictions count in this ladder alongside demerit convictions.

lines.text: Twelve in twelve, or eighteen in twenty-four: clinic.
Eighteen in twelve, or twenty-four in twenty-four: ninety-day suspension.

narration.text: Here is the trap: there are two point lines for drivers past eighteen, and the numbers overlap. Twelve points in twelve months, or eighteen in twenty-four months, orders a clinic, with a ninety-day suspension for skipping it. Eighteen points in twelve months, or twenty-four in twenty-four months, suspends the license for ninety days plus the clinic. So eighteen points means a clinic if it built up over twenty-four months, but a suspension if it built up over twelve. Twelve in twelve or eighteen in twenty-four orders the clinic, while eighteen in twelve or twenty-four in twenty-four suspends ninety days. Check both the total and the window.

lines.text: Can demand doctor or vision reports and retests.
Ends in suspension, restriction, periodic reports or closure.

narration.text: Medical review follows up reported doubts about a driver's physical or mental fitness, covering consciousness, perception, judgment and motor skills. It can demand reports from a doctor or a vision specialist, and retests. It ends in one of four ways: suspension, restriction, periodic reports, or a clean closure. Medical suspensions skip the legal presence proofs that other suspensions require. Compare a skipped clinic: skipped clinics suspend until done, while medical review can suspend, restrict, require periodic reports or close clean. So medical review starts from reported doubts about a driver's physical or mental fitness.

Here is a quick check: Zack is twenty-five and builds up eighteen points in twelve months. What follows? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a ninety-day suspension plus the clinic. Past eighteen, eighteen points in twelve months, or twenty-four in twenty-four months, suspends the license ninety days plus the clinic. If Zack's eighteen points had built up over twenty-four months instead, the result would be a clinic, with a ninety-day suspension only if he skipped it. The window changes the result even when the total is the same. Twelve in twelve means clinic, and eighteen in twelve means suspension.

lines.text: Three, four or six points per offense.
Under eighteen: clinic, ninety days, revocation.

narration.text: To close the lesson: DMV logs every court conviction and assigns three, four or six demerit points for traffic offenses, watched over twelve-month and twenty-four-month windows. Under eighteen, a first demerit or belt conviction orders a clinic, a second suspends ninety days, and a third revokes for a year or until eighteen. At eighteen or nineteen, any demerit or belt conviction orders a clinic. Past eighteen, twelve in twelve or eighteen in twenty-four orders a clinic, and eighteen in twelve or twenty-four in twenty-four suspends ninety days plus the clinic. Medical review can end in suspension, restriction, periodic reports or clean closure.

why_how.text: Registering a vehicle requires an insurance oath or an uninsured-vehicle fee.
Insurance failures and unpaid child support can each lead DMV to suspend.

scenario.text: Ivy drops her car insurance but keeps the license plates on the car.

reasoning.text: Breaking coverage without surrendering plates is one of the two insurance failures that draw suspension.

result.text: Ivy faces a suspension unless she keeps coverage or surrenders the plates.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can drop insurance and keep your plates without consequence.

correction.text: Breaking coverage without surrendering plates draws a suspension, as does skipping requested proof filings.

prompt.text: Ivy drops her insurance but keeps her plates. What can follow?

rationale.text: Insurance lapses suspend over missing proof filings or plates kept without coverage.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on insurance and support suspensions. When you register a vehicle, Virginia requires either an insurance oath or a fee for an uninsured vehicle. After that, two insurance failures can lead to a suspension. And outside of driving altogether, child-support enforcement can direct DMV to suspend a license. In this lesson we cover the registration requirement, the two insurance failures that draw suspension, and the child-support triggers. We will set the triggers side by side and compare them carefully.

lines.text: Or a five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee.

narration.text: Registering a vehicle requires an insurance oath or a five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee. So at registration you either swear the vehicle is insured or pay the uninsured-vehicle fee. Compare a rule from the last lesson about medical review: medical suspensions skip the legal presence proofs that other suspensions require. Put the two together: registration demands coverage proof or five hundred dollars, while medical suspensions uniquely skip presence proofs. The registration requirement is the starting point for the insurance rules in this lesson. Once a vehicle is registered, the next slide covers what happens when the coverage behind that oath is not kept up.

Here is the trap. A driver drops insurance, keeps the plates on the car, and assumes nothing will happen as long as the car is parked. The manual names two insurance failures that draw suspension: skipping requested proof filings, and breaking coverage without surrendering the plates. So if you end your coverage, the plates must be surrendered, and if DMV asks you to file proof of insurance, you must file it. Either failure on its own can lead to a suspension. The memory line is short: no coverage, no plates. Keeping the plates while dropping coverage is exactly the failure the manual describes.

lines.text: Arrears of ninety days or five thousand dollars.
Or dodging paternity and support process.

narration.text: Child-support enforcement can direct DMV to suspend a license for arrears of ninety days or five thousand dollars, or for dodging paternity and support process. Put the insurance and support triggers side by side: insurance lapses suspend over missing proof or kept plates, while support lapses suspend over ninety days or five thousand dollars in arrears, or dodged process. So DMV can suspend a license on child-support grounds. The ninety-day and five-thousand-dollar figures are the two arrears triggers, and dodging the paternity or support process is a third trigger that does not depend on any amount owed.

Here is a quick check: Ivy drops her car insurance but keeps the license plates on the car. What can follow? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a suspension. Breaking coverage without surrendering the plates is one of the two insurance failures that draw suspension; the other is skipping requested proof filings. If Ivy no longer wants coverage, the plates must be surrendered. And at registration, she would have had to give an insurance oath or pay the five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee. No coverage, no plates.

lines.text: Oath or five hundred dollars at registration.
Proof skipped or plates kept: suspension.
Support arrears or dodged process: suspension.

narration.text: To close the lesson: registering a vehicle requires an insurance oath or a five hundred dollar uninsured-vehicle fee. Two insurance failures draw suspension: skipping requested proof filings, and breaking coverage without surrendering the plates. Child-support enforcement can direct DMV to suspend for arrears of ninety days or five thousand dollars, or for dodging paternity and support process. And from the last lesson, remember that medical suspensions skip the legal presence proofs that other suspensions require. The memory line for insurance is: no coverage, no plates.

why_how.text: Driving in Virginia means consenting to breath tests, and refusing or failing one brings automatic suspension.
Open containers, a child aboard, driving while suspended, crashes and underage drinking each add penalties.

scenario.text: Max is stopped on probable cause and refuses the breath test; it is his first offense.

reasoning.text: Refusing the breath test or blowing point zero eight or more triggers an automatic suspension of seven days for a first offense.

result.text: Max's license is automatically suspended for seven days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can refuse a breath test without penalty.

correction.text: Driving consents to breath tests, and refusal or a BAC of point zero eight brings seven days, sixty days or hold until trial.

prompt.text: Max refuses the breath test on a first offense. How long is the automatic suspension?

rationale.text: Refusal or point zero eight brings seven days for a first offense, sixty days or until trial for a second, and until trial for a third.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on implied consent and alcohol penalties. Driving on Virginia roads means you have consented to breath tests in certain situations, and refusing or failing one brings an automatic suspension that grows with each offense. The manual then lists several penalties that are added on top: for open alcohol in the passenger area, for DUI with a child aboard, for driving during an alcohol suspension, for the cost of responders to a DUI crash, and for drivers under twenty-one. This lesson has many numbers, so we will group them by situation and finish by comparing the underage penalty with the first adult suspension.

lines.text: Driving consents to breath tests on demand.
After probable-cause stops with drink or drug suspicion.
Post-crash DUI arrests within three hours, no warrant.

narration.text: Driving on Virginia roads means you consent to breath tests on demand after probable-cause stops where drink or drug use is suspected. After a crash, a DUI arrest can be made within three hours without a warrant, anywhere. So the consent is part of the privilege of driving: by using Virginia roads, you have already agreed to the test in those situations. The three-hour window is the number to remember for post-crash arrests. The next slide covers what happens if a driver refuses the test, or takes it and blows point zero eight or more, because both lead to the same automatic suspension ladder.

lines.text: Second: sixty days or until trial.

narration.text: Here is the trap: refusing the breath test is not a way to avoid a penalty. Refusing the test, or blowing point zero eight or more, triggers an automatic suspension: seven days for a first offense, sixty days or until trial for a second, and held until trial for a third. Penalties from a conviction stack on top, and terms for multiple DUIs run consecutively. So driving consents to breath tests, and refusal or point zero eight brings seven days, sixty days, or a hold until trial. The memory line is: seven, sixty, until trial. Refusal and a high reading lead to the same ladder.

lines.text: Open, partly drunk alcohol in the passenger zone, with drinking signs.
DUI with a rider seventeen or under: five extra jail days.
Plus five hundred to one thousand dollars; eighty service hours on repeats.

narration.text: Open alcohol in the passenger area, which means the seats and anything within reach including an unlocked glovebox, partly drunk, with signs of drinking showing, earns a charge of drinking while operating. DUI with a rider aged seventeen or under adds a mandatory five extra jail days and an extra fine of five hundred to one thousand dollars, and on repeat offenses, eighty extra hours of community service, all on top of every base penalty. Put as a contrast: open container charges need set conditions, while child-aboard DUI stacks jail days and fines by repeat. The age in the child rule is seventeen or under.

lines.text: Driving on an alcohol suspension: car seized thirty days, plus ninety on conviction.
Repeat unlicensed driving: car held until licensed or three days.
DUI crash: billed up to one thousand dollars for responders.

narration.text: Driving during an alcohol suspension means the car is seized for thirty days on the spot, plus ninety more days on conviction. Repeat unlicensed operation holds the car until the driver is licensed or for three days, whichever ends first. And local law can bill a DUI crasher up to one thousand dollars for the responders the crash summons. So alcohol-suspension driving seizes the car thirty plus ninety days, repeat unlicensed driving holds it three days, and DUI wrecks can be billed up to a thousand dollars for responder costs. These penalties reach the car and the wallet, in addition to the license.

lines.text: BAC point zero two to point zero eight.
Plus five hundred dollar minimum fine or fifty-plus service hours.

narration.text: For drivers under twenty-one, drink-driving with a BAC from point zero two to point zero eight costs a one-year suspension from conviction, plus a mandatory minimum fine of five hundred dollars or at least fifty hours of community service. Compare the first adult automatic suspension: the underage penalty of a year plus a fine or service is harsher than a first adult administrative hold of seven days. So a level that would not reach the adult DUI line still carries a serious penalty for a driver under twenty-one. The two numbers to remember are the BAC range, point zero two to point zero eight, and the one-year suspension.

Here is a quick check: Max is stopped on probable cause, it is his first offense, and he refuses the breath test. How long is the automatic suspension? Work it out before reading on. The answer is seven days. Refusing the breath test, or blowing point zero eight or more, triggers an automatic suspension of seven days for a first offense, sixty days or until trial for a second, and until trial for a third. Max consented to the test by driving on Virginia roads, and any conviction penalties would stack on top of the automatic suspension. Seven, sixty, until trial.

To close the section: driving on Virginia roads consents to breath tests after probable-cause stops, and post-crash DUI arrests can be made within three hours without a warrant. Refusal or point zero eight brings seven days, sixty days or a hold until trial. Open, partly drunk alcohol in the passenger area with drinking signs earns a charge. DUI with a rider seventeen or under adds five jail days and a five hundred to one thousand dollar fine. Driving on an alcohol suspension seizes the car thirty days plus ninety on conviction, and DUI crashers can be billed up to one thousand dollars for responders. Under twenty-one, point zero two to point zero eight costs a one-year suspension.
